candidates.phrase: were inseparably joined together in one person, without conversion, composition, or confusion
candidates.rationale: Confession explicitly denies confusion of the two natures joined in Christ's one person, directly asserting the delimiter.
candidates.chunk_text: The Son of God, the second person in the Trinity, being very and eternal God, of one substance and equal with the Father, did, when the fullness of time was come, take upon him man’s nature, with all the essential properties, and common infirmities thereof, yet without sin; being conceived by the power of the Holy Ghost, in the womb of the virgin Mary, of her substance. So that two whole, perfect, and distinct natures, the Godhead and the manhood, were inseparably joined together in one person, without conversion, composition, or confusion. Which person is very God, and very man, yet one Christ, the only Mediator between God and man.

candidates.phrase: acts according to both natures, by each nature doing that which is proper to itself
candidates.rationale: Asserts each nature retains its own distinct operation within the union, a narrower affirmation of non-collapse of distinctions.
candidates.chunk_text: Christ, in the work of mediation, acts according to both natures, by each nature doing that which is proper to itself; yet, by reason of the unity of the person, that which is proper to one nature is sometimes in Scripture attributed to the person denominated by the other nature.

candidates.chunk_text: Who is the mediator of the covenant of grace? A. The only mediator of the covenant of grace is the Lord Jesus Christ, who, being the eternal Son of God, of one substance and equal with the Father, in the fullness of time became man, and so was and continues to be God and man, in two entire distinct natures, and one person, forever.

candidates.phrase: the proper works of each nature might be accepted of God
candidates.rationale: States each nature retains its own proper works within the one person, implying the distinct natures are not confused.
candidates.chunk_text: Why was it requisite that the mediator should be God and man in one person? A. It was requisite that the mediator, who was to reconcile God and man, should himself be both God and man, and this in one person, that the proper works of each nature might be accepted of God for us, and relied on by us, as the works of the whole person.

candidates.phrase: Christ's divinity is surely beyond the bounds of the humanity that has been taken on
candidates.rationale: Denies the natures are separated while affirming divinity remains beyond humanity's bounds, asserting the natures are distinct though united.
candidates.chunk_text: Q. If his humanity is not present wherever his divinity is, then aren’t the two natures of Christ separated from each other? A. Certainly not. Since divinity is not limited and is present everywhere, it is evident that Christ’s divinity is surely beyond the bounds of the humanity that has been taken on, but at the same time his divinity is in and remains personally united to his humanity. ( )

candidates.phrase: In his human nature Christ is not now on earth
candidates.rationale: Asserts Christ's humanity has its own limited property (locality) distinct from his divinity's omnipresence, maintaining distinction of natures.
candidates.chunk_text: Q. But isn’t Christ with us until the end of the world as he promised us? A. Christ is true human and true God. In his human nature Christ is not now on earth; but in his divinity, majesty, grace, and Spirit he is never absent from us.

candidates.phrase: by the power of his divinity, might bear the weight of God's wrath
candidates.rationale: Distinguishes divinity's power from humanity's suffering role in the mediator, preserving distinct properties of each nature in the union.
candidates.chunk_text: Q. Why must the mediator also be true God? A. So that the mediator, by the power of his divinity, might bear the weight of God’s wrath in his humanity and earn for us and restore to us righteousness and life.

candidates.locator: Article 19: The Two Natures of Christ
candidates.phrase: two natures united in a single person, with each nature retaining its own distinct properties
candidates.rationale: States the two natures remain united yet each keeps its own distinct properties, directly denying collapse of distinctions.
candidates.chunk_text: We believe that by being thus conceived the person of the Son has been inseparably united and joined together with human nature, in such a way that there are not two Sons of God, nor two persons, but two natures united in a single person, with each nature retaining its own distinct properties. Thus his divine nature has always remained uncreated, without beginning of days or end of life, filling heaven and earth. Christ’s human nature has not lost its properties but continues to have those of a creature— it has a beginning of days; it is of a finite nature and retains all that belongs to a real body. And even though he, by his resurrection, gave it immortality, that nonetheless did not change the reality of his human nature; for our salvation and resurrection depend also on the reality of his body. But these two natures are so united together in one person that they are not even separated by his death. So then, what he committed to his Father when he died was a real human spirit which left his body. But meanwhile his divine nature remained united with his human nature even when he was lying in the grave; and his deity never ceased to be in him, just as it was in him when he was a little child, though for a while it did not so reveal itself. These are the reasons why we confess him to be true God and truly human— true God in order to conquer death by his power, and truly human that he might die for us in the weakness of his flesh. 45

survivors.phrase: were inseparably joined together in one person, without conversion, composition, or confusion
survivors.rationale: Confession explicitly denies confusion of the two natures joined in Christ's one person, directly asserting the delimiter.
survivors.chunk_text: The Son of God, the second person in the Trinity, being very and eternal God, of one substance and equal with the Father, did, when the fullness of time was come, take upon him man’s nature, with all the essential properties, and common infirmities thereof, yet without sin; being conceived by the power of the Holy Ghost, in the womb of the virgin Mary, of her substance. So that two whole, perfect, and distinct natures, the Godhead and the manhood, were inseparably joined together in one person, without conversion, composition, or confusion. Which person is very God, and very man, yet one Christ, the only Mediator between God and man.

survivors.phrase: God and man in two distinct natures, and one person, forever
survivors.rationale: Affirms Christ as God and man in two distinct natures united in one person, denying collapse of the distinction between them.
survivors.chunk_text: Who is the redeemer of God’s elect? A. The only redeemer of God’s elect is the Lord Jesus Christ, who, being the eternal Son of God, became man, and so was, and continueth to be, God and man in two distinct natures, and one person, forever.

survivors.phrase: in two entire distinct natures, and one person, forever
survivors.rationale: Asserts Christ remains God and man in two entire distinct natures united in one person, denying any collapse of the natures.
survivors.chunk_text: Who is the mediator of the covenant of grace? A. The only mediator of the covenant of grace is the Lord Jesus Christ, who, being the eternal Son of God, of one substance and equal with the Father, in the fullness of time became man, and so was and continues to be God and man, in two entire distinct natures, and one person, forever.

survivors.locator: Book of Confessions 6.044 (Westminster Confession of Faith)
survivors.phrase: were inseparably joined together in one person, without conversion, composition, or confusion

survivors.chunk_text: 2. The Son of God, the second Person in the Trinity, being very and eternal God, of one substance, and equal with the Father, did, when the fullness of time was come, take upon him man’s nature, with all the essential properties and common infirmities thereof; yet without sin: being conceived by the power of the Holy Ghost, in the womb of the Virgin Mary, of her substance. survivors.phrase: Christ's divinity is surely beyond the bounds of the humanity that has been taken on
survivors.rationale: Denies the natures are separated while affirming divinity remains beyond humanity's bounds, asserting the natures are distinct though united.
survivors.chunk_text: Q. If his humanity is not present wherever his divinity is, then aren’t the two natures of Christ separated from each other? A. Certainly not. Since divinity is not limited and is present everywhere, it is evident that Christ’s divinity is surely beyond the bounds of the humanity that has been taken on, but at the same time his divinity is in and remains personally united to his humanity. ( )

survivors.locator: Article 19: The Two Natures of Christ
survivors.phrase: two natures united in a single person, with each nature retaining its own distinct properties
survivors.rationale: States the two natures remain united yet each keeps its own distinct properties, directly denying collapse of distinctions.
survivors.chunk_text: We believe that by being thus conceived the person of the Son has been inseparably united and joined together with human nature, in such a way that there are not two Sons of God, nor two persons, but two natures united in a single person, with each nature retaining its own distinct properties. Thus his divine nature has always remained uncreated, without beginning of days or end of life, filling heaven and earth. Christ’s human nature has not lost its properties but continues to have those of a creature— it has a beginning of days; it is of a finite nature and retains all that belongs to a real body. And even though he, by his resurrection, gave it immortality, that nonetheless did not change the reality of his human nature; for our salvation and resurrection depend also on the reality of his body. But these two natures are so united together in one person that they are not even separated by his death. So then, what he committed to his Father when he died was a real human spirit which left his body. But meanwhile his divine nature remained united with his human nature even when he was lying in the grave; and his deity never ceased to be in him, just as it was in him when he was a little child, though for a while it did not so reveal itself. These are the reasons why we confess him to be true God and truly human— true God in order to conquer death by his power, and truly human that he might die for us in the weakness of his flesh. 45

survivors.phrase: they are not absorbed, or confused, or mixed, but are united or joined together
survivors.rationale: States the divine and human natures in Christ are united without being confused, matching the without-confusion delimiter.
survivors.chunk_text: TWO NATURES IN CHRIST. We therefore acknowledge two natures or substances, the divine and the human, in one and the same Jesus Christ our Lord (Heb., ch. 2). And we say that these are bound and united with one another in such a way that they are not absorbed, or confused, or mixed, but are united or joined together in one person— the properties of the natures being unimpaired and permanent.

survivors.phrase: acts according to both natures, by each nature doing that which is proper to itself
survivors.rationale: Asserts each nature retains its own distinct operation within the union, a narrower affirmation of non-collapse of distinctions.
survivors.chunk_text: Christ, in the work of mediation, acts according to both natures, by each nature doing that which is proper to itself; yet, by reason of the unity of the person, that which is proper to one nature is sometimes in Scripture attributed to the person denominated by the other nature.

survivors.phrase: the proper works of each nature might be accepted of God
survivors.rationale: States each nature retains its own proper works within the one person, implying the distinct natures are not confused.
survivors.chunk_text: Why was it requisite that the mediator should be God and man in one person? A. It was requisite that the mediator, who was to reconcile God and man, should himself be both God and man, and this in one person, that the proper works of each nature might be accepted of God for us, and relied on by us, as the works of the whole person.
